summary.value: The paper studies the training dynamics of models trained with microscaling (MX) quantization in the forward and backward passes. MX formats (and other similar block scaled formats such as NVFP4) are become widely used for low precision training, making this a practical area to study. The paper studies this problem by training many models and considering a toy example with a student/teacher model setup. The paper finds that the main reason for loss spikes and divergence training is due to overflow in layernorm parameters during MX quantization, which can be mitigated by modifying the MX quantization algorithm.

strengths.value:
- The authors trained a large number of models to show that when applied "incorrectly," MX datatypes can cause training instability. 
- The minimal synthetic model is very interesting, as it is able to mostly model the effect of different norms and activation functions on training instabilities.

weaknesses.value:
- The main takeaway of this paper seems to not quantize layernorms, but people generally do not quantize non-decoder layer linear layers already. Can the authors explain why you would want to quantize things beyond linear layers? The point of using hardware supported datatypes for quantization is to accelerate compute bound matrix multiplications, and these operations are almost entirely contained in projection layers and self attention, neither of which appears to be source of training instabilities according to this paper.
- Since the main remedy appears to be avoiding overflow during rounding, I would have liked to see more experiments on different rounding methods that solve this. Increasing the exponent is just one way - https://aisystemcodesign.github.io/papers/FP4.pdf discusses more methods that get around this.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comments and feedback, and we sincerely appreciate their recognition of the synthetic model’s value in enabling our mechanistic analysis.  We address their concerns below.

# Weaknesses

**W1**
> The main takeaway of this paper seems to not quantize layernorms, but people generally do not quantize non-decoder layer linear layers already. Can the authors explain why you would want to quantize things beyond linear layers? The point of using hardware supported datatypes for quantization is to accelerate compute bound matrix multiplications, and these operations are almost entirely contained in projection layers and self attention, neither of which appears to be source of training instabilities according to this paper.

The reviewer asks why one would quantize components beyond large linear layers, noting that compute-bound operations are mainly in projections and attention. We respectfully clarify two key points regarding the scope of our work and the hardware context:

1. While we agree that a general practical heuristic is to keep LayerNorm parameters in higher precision (including other fixes), our contribution is not the heuristic itself but explaining why such fixes become necessary in block-scaled formats. The instability we observe is not due to the sensitivity of LayerNorm statistics (mean/variance accumulation) as noted in previous works, but to a failure mode unique to shared-scale quantization: the block exponent couples the different parameters, such that clustered weights collapse to a bin before any computation, injecting a persistent gradient bias. This mechanism is quite distinct from accumulation/outlier issues emphasized in prior work. Our goal was to highlight how this failure mode occurs, using LayerNorm affine weights as *one specific example* of where this mechanism is pronounced.

2. This mechanism is not exclusive to LayerNorm. As shown in Figure 3 (right), the same effect impacts a fraction of activations throughout the network. Even with LayerNorm kept in high precision, these activation effects can be sufficient to destabilize training (although they are subleading; see Appendix F). In practice, disabling LN-affine quantization widens the learning-rate stability window, but at larger learning rates closer to those used in full precision (1e-3), we find that activation-driven instabilities can still appear. This means that skipping LayerNorm quantization is not a complete fix, and that one must address the underlying shared-scale coupling to prevent activation-driven instabilities in the large projection layers the reviewer mentions.

We will clarify these points and better highlight that LayerNorm serves as an example of a more general shared-scale effect.

**W2**
> Since the main remedy appears to be avoiding overflow during rounding, I would have liked to see more experiments on different rounding methods that solve this. Increasing the exponent is just one way - https://aisystemcodesign.github.io/papers/FP4.pdf discusses more methods that get around this.

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this reference and apologize for the omission – we somehow missed it.  We will include it in revision. Comparing various exponent prescriptions is indeed very relevant. We are willing to run at least one comparison in the next version of the draft if it would affect your evaluation. However, due to limited GPU availability on our academic cluster especially during this rebuttal period, we cannot complete these experiments within the rebuttal window.

We thank the reviewer again for their feedback, which we will incorporate to improve our work.

comment.value:
I went through your paper again and its really not clear to me what the main contribution is. Your experiments and analysis conclude that the default MX algorithm induces clipping during rounding, which can cascade into catastrophic divergence during training. However, in actual hardware, users are free to choose any rounding algorithm they want, such as the one proposed by Tseng et al. that doesn't clip, or the ones I linked in the Meta paper that also don't clip. The default MX rounding algorithm isn't a "privileged" rounding algorithm in Blackwell in the sense that it isn't burned onto the chip or implementable faster than other choices of rounding algorithms, so the findings in your paper don't actually show that the MX *datatype* is bad, just that the default MX *rounding algorithm* is bad. However, this has been done before (by Tseng and the Meta paper), so there's not too much new here. 

Perhaps you could clarify if I grossly misread your paper or missed anything important. The minimal synthetic model does seem to be a new and interesting approach to analyzing instability for LLM training, but the findings from it are mostly already in the literature. 

> We are willing to run at least one comparison in the next version of the draft if it would affect your evaluation. However, due to limited GPU availability on our academic cluster especially during this rebuttal period, we cannot complete these experiments within the rebuttal window.

I don't think this alone would be sufficient for me to recommend acceptance, and it doesn't seem like you have enough resources to make these experiments a main part of the paper in the next week.

summary.value: The paper attempts a systematic study on the stability of MXFP8 format for training LLMs. Through extensive experiments on a proxy model, they find the instabilities to be the result of gradient bias due to quantization. This bias stems mainly from layer-norm weight distribution and sometimes other activations. Bridging to the LLM case, they suggest keeping the layer norm (and activations) in bfloat16, and only quantizing the forward pass.

strengths.value:
- The paper is generally well-written
- Systematic approach

weaknesses.value:
- While the study is interesting, the findings are not significant: in quantized/quantization-aware training, layer norms are generally skipped as they don't have significant memory or computation overhead (if implemented correctly).
- Some assumptions/conclusions are loose (see Questions below)

questions.value:
1. The fact that layer norm should be kept in high precision is not new, e.g., [1] shows even FP16 layer-norm is difficult (even before that for batch norm [2]). Additionally, to my knowledge, practical papers in quantization-aware training such as QuEST [3] already know not to touch the layer-norm layers. Even standard implementations of normalization layers make sure to operate in FP32, such as [4]. So my question is that what is the novelty in this paper's findings?

2. It's not clear to me why such proxy model is "good." In the authors' words: "we caution that stability in this minimal model as a necessary (though perhaps not sufficient) condition for stability in the full LM." Why is this a necessary condition? Note that this means if LLMs fail in a certain setting, then this proxy model will also fail.

3. Can you verify that you have FP32 master weights? Maybe I missed it, but I didn't find it explicitly in the paper.

4. Since the finding is that instability is due to gradient bias, how would the results look like if stochastic rounding is employed? Theoretically, quantization errors due to stochastic rounding should be unbiased. Although I understand it does not affect overflow.

5. Can you elaborate on why there is no layer-norm is the teacher?

6. How would your studies interact with Hadamard transformations [3], which is now common practice in QAT?

In the current state, despite the systematic investigation, I don't believe this paper offers any significant contribution.

[1] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.10553
[2] https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.03740
[3] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.05003
[4] https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/4d0b6758b90aa54e4077171e6d42c55e0c01c622/src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py#L64

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission1136 by Reviewer oB7k

comment.value:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their comments and constructive feedback.  We appreciate that they found the paper clearly written and our approach systematic.  We address their specific concerns and questions below.

# Weaknesses

**W1** / **Q1**
> While the study is interesting, the findings are not significant: in quantized/quantization-aware training, layer norms are generally skipped as they don't have significant memory or computation overhead (if implemented correctly).

> [...] what is the novelty in this paper's findings?


We respectfully disagree with the assessment that the findings are not significant based on standard QAT practices.  We address two key points below to clarify the scope and regime of our work.

First, we note that our study operates in the pre-training regime, where the model is trained from scratch with weights, activations, and gradients in standard low-precision formats (MX) to accelerate training throughput. This is distinct from Quantization-Aware Training (QAT), where gradients are often computed in higher precision, and the primary goal is to adapt a pre-trained model to a fixed quantization grid for inference.

Second, while it is true that general practice in QAT is to keep LayerNorms (and other sensitive components) in high precision, our contribution is not the generic advice to "keep LayerNorm in high precision." Rather, we aimed to identify a specific failure mode unique to block-scaling recipes, which has a different mechanistic origin than the issues described in the literature cited by the reviewer.  The cited papers (for example [1]) largely discuss overflow due to *accumulation* or outlier handling. By contrast, the overflow mechanism we identify comes from the recipe for computing shared exponents in block-scaling, which causes tightly clustered values (like LayerNorm affine *parameters*) to be clamped to the maximum representable number *before any computation even occurs*.  Our goal was to highlight the failure mode itself and LayerNorm is used only as a concrete example where this shared-scale effect is especially pronounced, not the central focus. We sincerely apologize that this did not come through clearly in the text and we will revise it to make the mechanism more explicit.

Our analysis also demonstrates that this mechanism is not exclusive to LayerNorms. As shown in Figure 3 (Right), it also affects a small fraction of activation values, which can independently destabilize training *even if* LayerNorms are kept in FP32 (although this effect is subleading compared to the LayerNorm effect; see Appendix F). In practice, disabling LN-affine quantization widens the learning-rate stability window, but when we train at larger learning rates closer to those used in full precision (1e-3), we find that activation-driven instabilities can still appear.  To the best of our knowledge, characterizing this specific origin of instability is novel. Understanding this mechanism is important for informing future block scaling recipes.  For example, recent proposals for low-precision training like [2] likely succeed by implicitly addressing the specific mechanism we explain in the paper.

We apologize for the missed references provided by the reviewer and will ensure they are included and discussed in the revised draft to better contextualize our contributions.

# Questions

**Q2**
> It's not clear to me why such proxy model is "good." In the authors' words: "we caution that stability in this minimal model as a necessary (though perhaps not sufficient) condition for stability in the full LM." Why is this a necessary condition? Note that this means if LLMs fail in a certain setting, then this proxy model will also fail.

The reviewer questions the necessity of the proxy model. To clarify:

1. We derived the proxy model by systematically stripping architectural components from the LLM (attention, embeddings, etc.) until the specific instability persisted. Therefore, stability in this proxy is a necessary condition because the proxy represents a core subset of the LLM’s operations. If the residual block arithmetic fails due to quantization bias in this simplified setting, the full Transformer (which necessarily relies on these blocks) will also fail.  This is desirable, as the proxy model is smaller and faster to train such that we can sweep over many hyperparameters, and can be trained on a simple synthetic task.
2. As noted in Worstman et al. [3], isolating failure modes in simplified settings such as in a proxy model can be a rigorous method for analyzing complex training dynamics. Our proxy allows us to mathematically characterize the bias (e.g., in Appendix B) and test phenomenological theories that would be computationally intractable on a full LLM. The fact that the proxy reproduces the instability signature of the LLM validates its utility.


[1] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.10553

[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08027

[3] https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14322

comment.value:
**Q3**
> Can you verify that you have FP32 master weights? Maybe I missed it, but I didn't find it explicitly in the paper.

That’s correct. We detail this in Appendix A.1 ("GEMM Simulation Settings"), our implementation accumulates in FP32, after which a single bfloat16 write-back operation is performed. We adhere to the standard MX recipe.

**Q4** + **Q6**
> Since the finding is that instability is due to gradient bias, how would the results look like if stochastic rounding is employed? Theoretically, quantization errors due to stochastic rounding should be unbiased. Although I understand it does not affect overflow.

> How would your studies interact with Hadamard transformations [3], which is now common practice in QAT?

Q4 is a very interesting question and also relates to the reviewer’s Q6 about Hadamard transformations.  The instability we observe stems from the shared scale definition in MX formats. When values in a block fall into the range defined in Eq. 2, they can still be clamped to the maximum representable number before rounding occurs (if the value is outside of the representable range during quantization).

However, we point to a recent promising work by Tseng et al. [4] where they propose an algorithm to train in MXFP4. They indeed propose a stochastic rounding method for MXFP4 alongside use of the Hadamard transform. However, their method requires a multiplicative shift to avoid the specific bias we characterize, although it is unclear how such a recipe adapted to MXFP8 would compare against other approaches, such as directly changing the block-scaling exponent scheme itself.  The purpose of our paper is to explain *exactly* where and how the bias can happen when using a shared block scale, and identify which architectural components are most sensitive to the coupling induced by quantization, which may inform future approaches.

**Q5**
> Can you elaborate on why there is no layer-norm is the teacher?

We removed LayerNorm from the teacher to assess how much "work" the student's LayerNorm was doing. The observation that removing LayerNorm from the student *stabilized* low-precision training (compared to high precision) provided the clue that the instability originated from the quantization of the affine parameters in LayerNorm, rather than the model's inability to fit the data distribution.

We thank the reviewer again for their valuable feedback which we will incoproate to improve our work. We will also include the suggested references as citations in order to clarify how our work differs from existing practices in the QAT literature.

[4] https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.20586

display_title: Official Review of Submission1136 by Reviewer 4KaL

summary.value:
This paper investigates the mechanistic origin of training instabilities observed when applying Microscaling (MX) low-precision formats (FP6/FP8) to LLM pretraining. The authors combine OLMo-based LLM experiments with controlled synthetic proxy models to demonstrate that the observed failures are not attributable to activation choices or hyperparameter settings, but instead arise from systematic quantization effects on LayerNorm affine parameters.

During training, LayerNorm affine parameters become highly clustered, and under MX block-scaled quantization, these values saturate into the same maximum bin due to shared scaling constraints. This saturation introduces persistent gradient bias, which accumulates across updates and ultimately leads to irreversible divergence in training loss. The paper provides empirical evidence for this failure mode, demonstrating both its emergence at LLM scale and its reproducibility within a simplified synthetic setting.

Building on this analysis, the authors propose practical stabilization strategies, including disabling LayerNorm affine quantization, keeping activations in bfloat16, and applying quantization only in the forward pass. Among these approaches, the configuration using MXFP8 (E4M3) weights and BF16 activations achieves validation performance comparable to full BF16 while avoiding instability.

strengths.value:
* The paper offers a clear mechanistic analysis of instability in MX-based low-precision training.
* It identifies a coherent failure chain in which LayerNorm affine parameters saturate under block-scale quantization, introducing gradient bias that ultimately triggers training divergence.
* The authors combine OLMo-based LLM experiments with a controlled synthetic proxy model, enabling both realistic evaluation and reproducible causal analysis.
* In-situ intervention experiments further provide empirical evidence that LayerNorm affine quantization is a primary causal factor behind the observed failures.
* The paper proposes practical and easily deployable mitigation strategies—such as disabling LN-affine quantization, using BF16 activations, or restricting quantization to the forward pass.
* These techniques restore stable training while matching the validation performance of full-BF16 systems, underscoring their practical utility.

weaknesses.value:
* Approaches such as disabling LN-affine quantization or increasing activation precision offer limited throughput benefits compared to standard BF16 training.
* Most empirical validation is conducted on OLMo-scale models, leaving generalization to frontier-scale systems uncertain.
* Although the paper reports activation overflow phenomena, its relative contribution is not quantitatively evaluated against the LayerNorm-induced mechanism, leaving the importance of this additional pathway insufficiently characterized.
* The paper identifies the core mechanism behind instability, but does not provide a systematic exploration of the conditions under which instability emerges—e.g., across compute scale, dataset size, or architectural variations—making it difficult to determine when MX training is expected to fail.
* Comparisons with other low-precision formats (e.g., per-channel scaling, PQ) are limited.

questions.value:
* Can the relative contributions of activation overflow and LN-affine saturation to the observed instability be quantitatively compared?
* Has this failure mechanism been evaluated in other architectures, such as MoE, MQA, or non-Transformer blocks?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission1136 by Reviewer 4KaL

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their comments and constructive feedback.  We also thank the reviewer for clearly articulating our strengths, from the mechanistic analysis and causal analysis of LN-affine saturations to the proxy/LLM evidence for the phenomenon we identify. We address their questions and concerns below:

# Weaknesses 

**W1**
> Approaches such as disabling LN-affine quantization or increasing activation precision offer limited throughput benefits compared to standard BF16 training.

We clarify that our primary contribution is a **mechanistic analysis** of a failure mode in block-scaled low-precision formats. Disabling LN-affine quantization is used to isolate the mechanism and widen the stability window and it does not, by itself, eliminate all residual effects (for example, activation overflow). That said, excluding LN-affine quantization leaves the vast majority of compute (forward and backward matmuls) in low precision, since LN-affine parameters constitute a negligible fraction of total parameters and FLOPs. At standard learning rates, additional steps such higher-precision activations may still be needed, though these fixes may be further refined with targeted, selective precision where sensitivity is highest.

Our intent is to clarify *why* instabilities occur and provide tools to practitioners to reason about block-scaling choices. As low-precision training scales to frontier systems, it is critical to understand why certain training recipes fail. Our work provides this kind of foundational understanding, which we believe has value independent of immediate throughput gains.

**W2**
> Most empirical validation is conducted on OLMo-scale models, leaving generalization to frontier-scale systems uncertain.

Frontier-scale pretraining is beyond academic compute. However, we do train up to ~1.7B parameters near Chinchilla-optimal and conduct nearly a thousand runs spanning 2e17 to 4.8e19 FLOPs, multiple datasets (e.g., FineWeb-Edu, StarCoder), formats (E4M3/E5M2/FP6), and hyperparameters (see Apps. F/G/J). We consistently observe the same failure mode. We will make these compute ranges and sweep counts explicit in the main text and emphasize that our claims are made at these scales.

Even at industrial labs, scaling laws and training recipes are typically validated at parameter scales below the scales of the largest runs.  This approach of studying mechanisms at tractable scales to inform larger deployments is not uncommon (see e.g., [1], on proxy models for transformer instabilities).

Finally, one of our core findings is that we demonstrate that instabilities *worsen* with scale (Fig. 1: larger models trained for longer diverge more frequently). This trend suggests our findings are *more* relevant at frontier scale, not less.

**W3**
> Although the paper reports activation overflow phenomena, its relative contribution is not quantitatively evaluated against the LayerNorm-induced mechanism, leaving the importance of this additional pathway insufficiently characterized.

We do provide this quantification in the paper, though we acknowledge it could be more prominently stated:

1. **Direct measurement (Fig. 3, right panel)**: Activation overflow affects ~0.5% of values in OLMo and ~1% in proxy models, compared to LayerNorm overflow affecting 50-75% of affine parameters in some layers.
2. **Ablation study (Appendix F, Fig. 12)**: We disable LN-affine quantization and measure residual instability:
   * At LR=2e-4: MXFP8 E4M3 remains almost completely stable without LN-affine quantization, indicating activation overflow is can only cause mild instabilities at moderate learning rates.  With LN-affine enabled at LR=2e-4: Rapid divergence, showing LN dominates the instability at typical learning rates
   * At LR=1e-3: Instabilities re-emerge even without LN-affine, demonstrating activation overflow becomes relevant at higher learning rates

**W4**
> The paper identifies the core mechanism behind instability, but does not provide a systematic exploration of the conditions under which instability emerges [...]

We believe we *do* provide this exploration, but it may be insufficiently highlighted within the text:

We performed nearly one thousand model training runs, with sweeps ranging from 2×10^17 to 4.8×10^19 FLOPs (Section 3, Appendix G) across two common pretraining datasets: FineWeb-Edu (Fig. 1) and StarCoder (Appendix J, Fig. 18), as well as several architectural variations:
* Depths: 3-8 layers (proxy), 6-24 layers (OLMo)
* Widths: 64-1024 (proxy), 20M-1.7B params (OLMo)
* Activations: ReLU, GeLU, SwiGLU (Fig. 2) Precision formats: MXFP6 (E2M3, E3M2), MXFP8 (E4M3, E5M2) (Appendix J)

We find that instabilities emerge across all tested configurations when the compute budget exceeds a threshold. This universality is precisely why we focus on the underlying mechanism rather than configuration-specific fixes

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14322

**W5**
> Comparisons with other low-precision formats (e.g., per-channel scaling, PQ) are limited.

The scope of our paper is primarily the failure mode specific to block-scaled, shared-exponent formats (MX). The core issue we analyze is the shared exponent and how the exponent prescription couples values within a block. Per-channel scaling is the extreme case where the block size equals the channel/row length. Increasing block size preserves the coupling and typically exacerbates loss of resolution within the group. Thus, comparisons to per-channel probe a different point in the same design space and do not test a mechanism that removes shared exponents. We will clarify this distinction and the practical constraint that MX hardware paths use fixed small blocks (i.e., 32).

PQ/centroid methods typically rely on codebook lookups and without specialized kernels that operate directly in the quantized domain, training-time GEMMs require dequantization, incurring substantial overhead. To our knowledge, PQ is mainly used for inference compression rather than end-to-end pretraining at scale. As such, it does not exhibit the same shared-exponent mechanism we study and is outside our empirical scope.

We’ll state this limitation explicitly in the revision.  Our results characterize the shared-scale block-quantization regime and formats that avoid shared exponents (e.g., per-channel) or use centroid codebooks (PQ) have different trade-offs, but they do not test the same instability mechanism.

# Questions

**Q1**
> Can the relative contributions of activation overflow and LN-affine saturation to the observed instability be quantitatively compared?

Addressed under W3 above.

**Q2**
> Has this failure mechanism been evaluated in other architectures, such as MoE, MQA, or non-Transformer blocks?

MoEs: We study only dense models. However, since MoE architectures involve similar structural components as the dense setting (FFNs, attention, etc.), we expect our analysis should hold for MoEs as well.

MQA/GQA: As noted in Appendix D, attention mechanisms are *not* the primary source of instability.  We find that it is the FFN LayerNorms which dominate (Fig. 3, middle). MQA simply reduces the number of attention heads, so we do not expect qualitative differences.

Non-Transformer blocks: We do not evaluate non-Transformer architectures (e.g., SSMs, hybrid models). This is indeed an important and interesting direction for future work, especially as architectures diversify. The core mechanism (shared-scale overflow from clustered parameters) may generalize, but verification is needed.
